name: Wano
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, final (final stress), not in the strict set' matches both primary sources: stress is word-final including suffixes, penultimate only when an enclitic (=a, =o 'pausal') follows, i.e. final on the affixal word with enclitics outside the stress domain. The deciding work is a 2017 630-pp Oxford reference grammar, the best and most recent description; the 2007 SIL phonology by the same author agrees. No contradicting source exists in Glottolog or on the web. Housekeeping only: move the 'sources' text into quote/cite, set loc = 'sec. 2.7, p. 64 (p. 100)', register the two copies we hold, assign an strength of the evidence; optionally code domain (suffixes stress-bearing, enclitics extrametrical; the domain quotation from p. 64 'Unlike cliticization, stress remains final-syllable in affixation.. the affix takes the stress') and note that Burung 2007 p. 46 transcribes secondary stress on σ2 of 4-syllable wo

sources.citation: Burung, Willem. 2017. A grammar of Wano. DPhil thesis, University of Oxford, sec. 2.7 Word Stress (ORA PDF, full text extracted)
sources.quote: To conclude, Wano stress is always word-final. In terms of cliticization, stress remains in the same syllable, thus resulting in penultimate stress.
sources.locator: sec. 2.7 Word Stress, pp. 63-64 (pp. 99-100); concluding quote p. 64
sources.note: The deciding source itself; catalog 'held' list was empty, so the file was placed in our files now (quote verified p. 64).

sources.citation: Burung, Willem. 2007. The Phonology of Wano. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2007-003. Dallas: SIL International. 101 pp. (open, sil.org/resources/archives/7846)
sources.quote: 'The stress is always syllable final, encountered in any polysyllabic word. In terms of morphophonology, stress may occur on the initial syllable (as in bok, »bok-o 'good-pausal') or penultimate syllable (a»mok, a»mok-o).' Four-syllable examples are transcribed with a secondary stress on σ2: /na.ka.mpu.tu/ [na«ƒabu»Ru] 'pumpkin', [bu«RiCa»ja] 'k.o. yam', [ta«baRa»ƒWi] 'cricket'. 'Stress is non-phonemic.'
sources.locator: sec. 8 Word Stress, p. 46 (p. 46); also abstract-area statement at the text 'stress falls on the final syllable'
sources.note: Only other descriptive work in Glottolog; independent earlier statement of final stress (p. 46) and the only place secondary stress is transcribed (σ2 in 4-syllable words) — useful if the secondary-stress rule is ever coded.
